title: The Toasty Riddle
markdown:
Iris the rabbit adored order. Her burrow proved it. Dandelion roots sat sorted by colour, palest yellow to richest gold. Dewdrops sparkled in a line by size. Her carrot stash was a masterpiece: every carrot, plump or tapered, pointing exactly north-west.

Today order had taken a singed tumble. Between a round orange carrot and a slender one with a jaunty green top lay a piece of parchment — old, edges as if they'd met a birthday candle, smelling of burnt sugar and, Iris thought with a shiver, disappointment.

It was a document about the annual village pie-eating contest. Ordinary local history. Not the sort of thing one kept among prime specimens. Frankly, a mess.

Milo the mole poked from his tunnel, whiskers twitching, spectacles precarious. "Iris, what's that funny-looking leaf? It looks a bit… toasty."

Iris sighed, dry leaves of a sound. "It's not a leaf. It's a historical document. Rather messy."

She lifted it gingerly. Milo nudged closer. Spectacles slipped. "Look! Words inside the burnt bits. It's a riddle!"

Where shiny things do gleam and gleam,
And tales are spun, it would seem,
A secret talent, yet untold,
Makes spirits bright and hearts so bold.

Iris's brow furrowed. Her filing-mind whirred like a clockwork mouse. "Shiny things… tales… Mrs. Thread has so many shiny things. Perhaps she would know."

Mrs. Thread's burrow was more museum than home. Polished pebbles lined the path. The sitting room shone with antique thimbles. She was buffing an ornate silver one when they arrived; metal clinked, musical.

"Hello dears! This one belonged to my Great Auntie Beatrice. She could stitch a barn door shut in under an hour, or so the legend goes. Imagine the drafts she saved us from!"

"We found a riddle," Milo explained, nearly tripping. "A secret talent that makes spirits bright."

Mrs. Thread's eyes twinkled like doorknobs. She tapped a thimble, then, with a flourish, set a lustrous gold one right on Iris's parchment. "I'm sure I don't recall offhand. Now this thimble has a tiny portrait of the Mayor of 1888. You can almost see his formidable moustache."

The riddle vanished under gold. Iris felt a flutter of frustration. Not orderly. Then a less orderly thought bloomed: she did not need to be told. She was good at puzzles.

"Thank you. We'll look for more shiny things. They might jog our memories."

They left. Iris's mind raced, not with carrot lines but with the riddle. Making spirits bright. She had thought of herself as tidy, not cheerful. What if the talent was making others cheerful — a quiet sort of useful?

Back near Milo's tunnel he excavated with enthusiasm, soil flying. A comical thump: a wobbly, brightly painted wooden leg, a prop from an old village play, blocking their path and casting a silly shadow.

"Oh dear." Milo's spectacles fogged. "I've made a mess. I was trying to help."

Iris did not sigh. She looked at the leg, at his dusty earnest face, at the riddle's line about bright spirits. "Maybe this wobbly leg is part of the history too. An unsteady part." She moved the prop. A faint imprint waited in the earth. "Another clue!"

A buried stone, smoothed by time: Where laughter echoes, and steps do stray, the true joy of yesterday.

"Laughter echoes?" Milo's whiskers quivered. "Steps stray — like when you trip over a root?"

Iris clicked. "The old village hall. They had dances. Jokes. Wobbly-kneed steps. That's where laughter echoes!" Surprise delighted her. It was more exciting than aligned carrots.

They hurried to the old village hall, its tall wooden doors creaking with the weight of years. Dust motes danced in the few shafts of sunlight that managed the grimy windows. The air hung thick with forgotten paper and dried flowers. Sunlight, gritty with dust, painted hazy stripes across the floor. The dry wood groaned with every cautious step. Inside, piled high on a forgotten shelf, they found a treasure trove of faded photographs and brittle yellowed diaries. There was a photograph of a villager attempting to balance seventeen teacups on his head, tongue sticking out in concentration. There was a diary entry detailing a fierce, clearly hilarious competition for the Most Enthusiastic Sneeze. And there was a photograph of villagers in an energetic dance-off, knees bent at such precarious angles they looked as if they might wobble away.

Iris looked at the earnest, slightly silly faces. They had not been worried about perfect order. They had been busy making one another laugh.

That was the talent. Not grand. Hilariously ordinary: finding the funny and sharing it.

Milo was already attempting to balance a dusty feather on his nose. Iris felt a quiet joy bubble. Her carrots still pointed north-west. She did not need her heart filed beside them.

"I wonder," she said, whiskers happy, "whether this year's pie contest still wants a sneeze champion — and whether a carrot pointing south-east, just one, would count as a joke or a crisis."

Milo's feather fell. He declared it a joke, which, as historical documents went, was easier to live with than burnt sugar.
